source: Maier, Bartos, Stanley, Shanks, Harris, Wagenmakers (2022) No evidence for nudging after adjusting for publication bias
finding: Re-analysis of the Mertens nudge meta-analysis. The raw average nudge effect is medium. After correcting for publication bias it shrinks to about zero.
numbers: Unadjusted random-effects d=0.43 [0.38,0.48]. Robust Bayesian model average, all studies: d=0.04 [0.00,0.14], BF01=0.95. Most precise studies only: d=0.11 [0.00,0.24], BF01=0.31. Egger b=2.10 (called severe).
limits: Overall result is ambiguous, not proof of zero (BF01 near 1). Depends on bias-model assumptions; Mertens et al. dispute it.
agent_relevance: Do not trust a headline average for a structural intervention. Expect the real gain of any one scaffold nudge to be far below the published effect.
quote: after correcting for this bias, no evidence remains that nudges are effective as tools for behaviour change

source: Maier, Bartos, Stanley, Shanks, Harris, Wagenmakers (2022) No evidence for nudging after adjusting for publication bias (by category)
finding: Split by Mertens' three nudge types: information nudges show strong evidence of no effect, assistance nudges also, structure nudges (defaults, effort changes) are the only ambiguous group.
numbers: Bias-adjusted: Information d=0.00 [0.00,0.00], BF01=33.84 (all) and 10.57 (precise). Assistance d=0.01 [0.00,0.07], BF01=9.05 and 8.00. Structure d=0.12 [0.00,0.43], BF01=1.12 and 0.33. Publication bias evidence BFpb>10 in every domain except food (precise BFpb=2.49).
limits: Structure result has a wide interval; food domain is the least biased.
agent_relevance: Changes to the structure of the choice (what is the default, how many steps) are more likely to work than reminders or advice. Favour structure inside the scaffold over exhortation.

source: Mertens, Herberz, Hahnel, Brosch (2022) Reply to Maier et al., Szaszi et al., and Bakdash and Marusich: The present and future of choice architecture research
finding: The original authors concede publication bias and unexplained heterogeneity, but defend a real, smaller effect.
numbers: Original meta-analysis: d=0.43 over more than 200 studies. Egger b=2.10, 95% CI [1.31,2.89], t(332)=5.22, p<0.001. Own sensitivity analysis: d=0.31 under moderate bias, d=0.08 under severe bias.
limits: Their dataset lacked information to test many moderators. They call for preregistered, powered studies and publishing nulls.
agent_relevance: The honest planning range for nudge-style gains is d 0.08 to 0.31, not 0.43. Measure our own effect with our own benchmark.

source: Szaszi, Higney, Charlton, Gelman, Ziano, Aczel, Goldstein, Yeager, Tipton (2022) No reason to expect large and consistent effects of nudge interventions
finding: Independent bias corrections agree the effect is small, and heterogeneity is huge. The paper argues the average is the wrong thing to study.
numbers: Unadjusted d=0.43. Severe-bias adjusted d=0.08; moderate d=0.31. Andrews-Kasy d=-0.01 (SE 0.02). WAAP (powered studies only) d=0.07 (SE 0.03). Trim and fill d=0.08 (SE 0.03). Under severe bias 95% of study effects lie within +/-1.00 of 0.08.
limits: Letter, no formal prediction interval, no study count in the letter. Notes defaults as an exception to inconsistent effects.
agent_relevance: The same nudge can help, do nothing or backfire by context. Gate any scaffold nudge on a held-out check per task type, not on a general claim.
quote: we see no reason to expect large and consistent effects

source: Szaszi, Higney, Charlton, Gelman, Ziano, Aczel, Goldstein, Yeager, Tipton (2022) No reason to expect large and consistent effects of nudge interventions (moderator and heterogeneity argument)
finding: Shows variability in nudge effects across domains, populations and places, with part of the variability coming from variability in publication bias itself.
numbers: Effect heterogeneity spans roughly +/-1 SD around the small bias-corrected mean (see b04).
limits: Argument paper, not a new dataset.
agent_relevance: Report the spread of the effect across task types, not only the mean.
quote: with much of this variability possibly arising from variability in publication bias itself

source: DellaVigna and Linos (2022) RCTs to Scale: Comprehensive Evidence from Two Nudge Units (Econometrica)
finding: Not opened this session (PDF fetches failed; numbers recalled from memory, must be verified). Two government nudge units ran 126 trials with no selective publication. The average effect was far smaller than in published academic nudge papers.
numbers: Recalled: 126 trials, about 23 million people; nudge-unit average about 1.4 percentage points vs about 8.7 for academic papers. VERIFY.
limits: Unopened; treat figures as unverified.
agent_relevance: If correct, this is the best field estimate of the real size of nudges at scale: an order of magnitude below the literature.

source: Jachimowicz, Duncan, Weber, Johnson (2019) When and why defaults influence decisions: a meta-analysis (Behavioural Public Policy)
finding: Not opened (publisher paywall). Defaults are the most robust nudge; effect is moderated by whether people endorse the default and by effort and loss framing.
numbers: Recalled: 58 studies, 73 effect sizes, overall d about 0.68. VERIFY.
limits: Unopened. Published-effect inflation (see b01-b04) may apply, but Szaszi et al. single out defaults as the exception.
agent_relevance: A default in the scaffold (for example, a mandatory base-rate step the model must actively skip) is the best-supported structural lever.

source: Flyvbjerg (2013) Quality Control and Due Diligence in Project Management: Getting Decisions Right by Taking the Outside View (arXiv 1302.2544)
finding: Describes the planning fallacy and the outside view as the cure. Reference class benchmark applied to a multibillion-dollar rail project shows the inside-view forecast gave a far too narrow range.
numbers: Benchmark of 61 rail demand forecasts: SD of accuracy 33% vs 9.1% in the project downside case; 95% confidence shortfall 85% vs 15%; chance of 15%+ shortfall 80% vs 5%.
limits: Case study with one project; benchmark built by the author's group. Anonymised project, no hold-out test of reference class forecasting itself.
agent_relevance: This is the concrete form of the outside view: take the class record and the class spread, then compare your own estimate of range. Widen the agent's stated uncertainty to the class SD.

source: Flyvbjerg (2013) Quality Control and Due Diligence in Project Management: Getting Decisions Right by Taking the Outside View (arXiv 1302.2544) (rail demand record)
finding: Rail demand forecasts are biased high on average in a large sample; the bias is stable.
numbers: 27 rail projects (Flyvbjerg et al. 2005): actual/forecast first-year demand mean 0.61, SD 0.52. Without 2 outliers actual demand is 51.4% below forecast, equal to 106% overestimate. Two forecaster track records were 500% and 175% first-year overestimates.
limits: Selected transport sample; two statistical outliers removed; different from software or reasoning tasks.
agent_relevance: Base rate for the agent's own class (its past plans of this type) beats its story about the present case.

source: Flyvbjerg (2013) Quality Control and Due Diligence in Project Management: Getting Decisions Right by Taking the Outside View (arXiv 1302.2544) (Lovallo and Kahneman student experiment, as reported)
finding: Asking students about the outside view first made forecasts more realistic but still too optimistic.
numbers: Control students expected to beat 84% of peers (logically impossible). A prior outside-view prompt cut expected performance ratings by about 20%, still overconfident. Source in the text: Lovallo and Kahneman 2003; Buehler, Griffin and Ross 1994.
limits: Secondary report of the experiment; cell sizes not given here.
agent_relevance: Outside view prompts reduce but do not remove optimism: use as a prior correction, then add a check.

source: Flyvbjerg (2013) Quality Control and Due Diligence in Project Management: Getting Decisions Right by Taking the Outside View (arXiv 1302.2544) (conditions where the outside view works)
finding: Argues the outside view only gets used when incentives reward accurate forecasts; where forecasters have a stake in optimism, incentives and mandatory benchmarks are needed.
numbers: No numeric result. The comparative advantage is largest for non-routine projects and where reference data exist.
limits: Opinion of the author; no controlled test.
agent_relevance: Make the base-rate step code-enforced, not left to the model's goodwill (matches G1/G3 spirit).
quote: for de-biasing to take place, incentives and methods for quality control of projects and decisions must be in place

source: Halawi, Zhang, Wang, Jiang, Steinhardt (2024) Approaching Human-Level Forecasting with Language Models (arXiv 2402.18563)
finding: Retrieval plus reasoning scratchpad that explicitly asks for historical base rates and a check for over/under-confidence. System nearly matches the human crowd but does not beat it.
numbers: Brier .179 vs human crowd .149 on the test set; accuracy 71.5% vs 77.0%; best plain GPT-4 baseline .208; unskilled 0.5 forecast .250. Without fine-tuning and without retrieval .206. A weaker ablation .186.
limits: The base-rate instruction is one part of a larger prompt; no ablation isolates it. The crowd is better when it is very confident (below .05).
agent_relevance: The best-documented LLM pipeline that uses a base-rate step is still below the crowd. Reference class prompting alone is not enough; retrieval and aggregation matter more.
quote: consider historical base rates (Tetlock and Gardner, 2015)

source: Halawi, Zhang, Wang, Jiang, Steinhardt (2024) Approaching Human-Level Forecasting with Language Models (arXiv 2402.18563) (where the system beats the crowd)
finding: System is better on uncertain questions and when many articles retrieved; worse where the crowd is highly confident.
numbers: When crowd predictions are .3 to .7, system Brier .199 vs crowd .246. By platform: INFER .134 vs .104; Polymarket .193 vs .157; Manifold .247 vs .310 (system better).
limits: Standard errors large on small platforms (Manifold SE .053).
agent_relevance: Base-rate anchoring may help most on the hardest items, where a gate adds value.

source: Schoenegger, Tuminauskaite, Park, Tetlock (2024) Wisdom of the Silicon Crowd (arXiv 2402.19379)
finding: A crowd of 12 LLMs matches a human crowd on binary forecasts. Models show an acquiescence bias toward yes. Exposure to the human median improves them.
numbers: 31 binary questions, 925 human forecasters vs 12 LLMs: not statistically different from the human crowd; equivalent within medium-effect bounds. Study 2: GPT-4 and Claude 2 accuracy improved 17% to 28% after seeing the human median; averaging human and machine was better still.
limits: Only 31 questions; one tournament; mean model prediction significantly above 50% despite an almost even split of outcomes.
agent_relevance: The agent analogue of an outside-view anchor is an external reference value; it helps, and aggregation of independent sources helps more. Beware yes-bias.

source: Echterhoff, Liu, Alessa, McAuley, He (2024) Cognitive Bias in Decision-Making with LLMs (BiasBuster, arXiv 2403.00811)
finding: Three prompt-level debiasers (awareness, few-shot contrastive/counterfactual, self-help rewriting) tested on four models and five biases. Results are mixed and model dependent.
numbers: 13,465 prompts. Anchoring distance d: GPT-4 baseline 0.250, awareness 0.105, contrastive 0.300, counterfactual 0.383, self-help 0.283. GPT-3.5 baseline 0.362, awareness 0.200. Framing delta GPT-3.5 0.165, awareness 0.035; GPT-4 -0.405, awareness -0.470 (worse).
limits: Synthetic admissions data; the Llama-2 models failed to follow few-shot instructions (rates 0 or 1). GPT-4 and GPT-3.5 framing/group tests only 400 prompts each.
agent_relevance: A named-bias reminder helped anchoring, but few-shot and self-help sometimes made things worse. Test every debias prompt per model.

source: Echterhoff, Liu, Alessa, McAuley, He (2024) Cognitive Bias in Decision-Making with LLMs (BiasBuster, arXiv 2403.00811) (self-help)
finding: Self-help, where the model rewrites its own prompt, works for strong models only.
numbers: Self-help leaves 0% biased group-attribution prompts and 2.7% biased framing prompts for GPT-4; GPT-3.5 still 17.2% framing and 8.5% status quo biased. Anchoring answers changed in 5.2% (GPT-3.5), 17.5% (GPT-4), 52.1% (Llama-2-13b), 39.9% (Llama-2-7b).
limits: Authors discourage use in high-stakes decisions; small-model changes are mostly noise rather than debiasing.
agent_relevance: Self-rewrite of the question is a cheap structural debiaser only when the model is strong.

source: Cognitive Biases in Large Language Models: A Survey and Mitigation Experiments (arXiv 2412.00323)
finding: Tests awareness reminder (AwaRe) and social projection (SoPro) on CoBBLEr. Naming the bias helps broadly; SoPro does not.
numbers: GPT-3.5 and GPT-4, 50 questions from 16 models, about 12,000 evaluations per bias. Bandwagon: GPT-3.5 0.524 baseline, AwaRe 0.260, SoPro 0.955 (worse). GPT-4 0.214, AwaRe 0.142. Order bias: no method gave a meaningful change. Valid output GPT-3.5 attentional test 0.713 baseline, 0.873 AwaRe, 0.472 SoPro.
limits: No statistical tests reported; the text claims AwaRe helps order bias but the table shows 0.200 to 0.191. Two models only.
agent_relevance: Telling the model which bias it has can reduce it, but needs the bias named in advance; order and position effects need code (shuffling), not prompts.

source: Zhong, Wang, Cao, Sun (2025) Balancing Rigor and Utility: Mitigating Cognitive Biases in LLMs for Multiple-Choice Questions (arXiv 2406.10999)
finding: A fixed list of human biases tested; adding an abstain option and a specific-bias inspection prompt cuts errors. Base rate neglect is a large failure in all three models on the standard prompt.
numbers: BRU set, 205 questions. Standard prompt, base rate fallacy (40 items): GPT-4 correct 15.0% (wrong 65.0%, other 20.0%); Gemini 1.0 Pro 15.0% (wrong 80.0%); LLaMA3-70B 10.0% (wrong 85.0%). Abstention plus specific-bias inspection: best accuracy 93.5% and error 3.9%; GPT-4 error near 3.9%, Gemini 6.3%.
limits: Authors built the set; correct means matching an expert-labelled rational-deviation answer. Bias detection by GPT-4o names the exact bias 65% of the time, 80% cumulative.
agent_relevance: Base-rate neglect is a measured, serious LLM weakness (10 to 15% correct), so the S0/S7 outside view gate has headroom. Allow the agent to abstain when the base rate and the case evidence conflict.

source: Zhong, Wang, Cao, Sun (2025) Balancing Rigor and Utility: Mitigating Cognitive Biases in LLMs for Multiple-Choice Questions (arXiv 2406.10999) (all biases)
finding: Per-bias spread on the standard prompt shows which biases need structure.
numbers: Standard prompt, GPT-4 correct: gambler's 75.0%, sample-size insensitivity 93.3%, conjunction 46.7%, anchoring 50.0%, overconfidence 10.0%, regression 14.3%, sunk cost 0.0%; total 36.1% (205 items). LLaMA3-70B sample-size insensitivity 6.7%.
limits: Same BRU set; small cell sizes (15 to 40 items).
agent_relevance: Overconfidence, regression to the mean and base rates are the weak points a base-rate gate should target.

source: Valencia-Clavijo (2025) Anchors in the Machine: Behavioral and Attributional Evidence of Anchoring Bias in LLMs (arXiv 2511.05766)
finding: Anchoring shifts whole output probability distributions in small open models, so it is a probability effect, not a surface imitation.
numbers: Six open models: robust effects in Gemma-2B, Phi-2, Llama-2-7B; variable in GPT-2, Falcon-RW-1B, GPT-Neo-125M. Attribution effects vary with prompt design.
limits: Small, old open models; no mitigation tested; no commercial models.
agent_relevance: An anchor placed in the prompt (including a base rate we supply) will move the model; choose the anchor carefully and place it after the problem own evidence when independence matters.

source: Li, Wang, Zhang, Zhu, Hou, Lian, Luo, Yang, Xie (2023) Large Language Models Understand and Can Be Enhanced by Emotional Stimuli (EmotionPrompt, arXiv 2307.11760)
finding: Adding stakes sentences such as This is very important to my career lifted scores in several models. This is the closest LLM analogue of an incentive.
numbers: 45 tasks, 6 models incl. ChatGPT and GPT-4: relative improvement 8.00% on Instruction Induction and 115% on BIG-Bench. Human study, 106 participants: 10.9% average gain on performance, truthfulness and responsibility. EP02 beat the worst stimulus by 6.06% on Instruction Induction.
limits: Gains concentrated in weak baselines (the 115% is relative to a low base); sensitive to prompt wording. Later replication results not read this session.
agent_relevance: Stakes sentences are cheap but not structural. If used, test on our own benchmark and do not stack them with checks.

source: Bsharat, Myrzakhan, Shen (2023) Principled Instructions Are All You Need (ATLAS, arXiv 2312.16171)
finding: Contains a principle to promise a tip for a better solution among 26 prompt rules. The paper reports only pooled results across principles, not the tip rule alone.
numbers: 26 principles; GPT-4 average improvement 57.7% in quality and 36.4% in accuracy on the ATLAS set; gains larger with model size (above 20 points from LLaMA-2-7B to GPT-4).
limits: Hand-built benchmark by the same authors; no isolated tip result in the text I read; the incentive claim is not verified.
agent_relevance: Do not rely on money or tip prompts. Weak evidence that an incentive sentence changes effort in a model.

source: Lerner and Tetlock (1999) Accounting for the effects of accountability (Psychological Bulletin)
finding: Not opened. Recalled: accountability helps only when the audience view is unknown, the person expects to justify the decision, and accountability is known before the evidence is seen. Otherwise it can raise bias.
numbers: No numbers recalled with confidence.
limits: Unopened; conditions listed from memory.
agent_relevance: For the agent, a justify-to-an-unknown-critic step before it forms the answer is the analogue; a known-preference audience (the user) would increase sycophancy.

source: Camerer and Hogarth (1999) The effects of financial incentives in experiments (J. Risk and Uncertainty)
finding: Not opened. Recalled: incentives raise effort and cut variance in tasks where effort helps but rarely change systematic biases such as anchoring or framing, and can hurt in tasks needing insight.
numbers: Recalled: about 74 studies reviewed; no pooled effect. VERIFY.
limits: Unopened; recall only.
agent_relevance: Reward in a prompt could raise diligence but should not be expected to fix bias; supports putting structure rather than stakes in the scaffold.

source: Halawi et al. (2024) Approaching Human-Level Forecasting with Language Models (arXiv 2402.18563), ablations
finding: Most of the gain over a plain model comes from retrieval and fine-tuning, not from the prompt wording alone. Without both, the pipeline falls back to the plain baseline.
numbers: Full system Brier .179. Ablated variant .186 (+.007). No fine-tuning and no retrieval: .206, about the same as the best plain GPT-4 baseline .208.
limits: The base-rate instruction is never ablated by itself.
agent_relevance: A prompt that says think of base rates is not the same as supplying the class record. Supply the record from code (retrieved past cases), as the outside view needs data.
